strengths: The paper targets an important and timely deployment bottleneck for reasoning LLMs: long chain-of-thought decoding makes KV cache memory a first-order constraint, and existing token-dropping/retrieval-head methods plausibly fail in this setting.

The proposed method is conceptually clear: freeze the LLM, learn per-layer/per-head gates between full and streaming attention using GRPO with a sparsity penalty, and then allocate full KV cache to the heads with high learned gate values. This is a reasonable and technically grounded way to connect compression decisions to downstream reasoning reward.

Empirical results are fairly broad for a systems/efficiency paper at this scale: two 7B/8B reasoning models, four benchmarks spanning math and code, multiple sparsity levels, and comparisons to token-dropping and head-reallocation baselines. RLKV consistently improves over baselines, especially at moderate sparsity.

The paper includes useful ablations for adaptive penalty weighting, self-distillation sampling, and the L1 penalty strength, and these help justify the stabilization choices rather than presenting the RL component as a black box.

The analysis comparing learned reasoning heads against retrieval heads is a useful interpretability angle. The masking/replacement experiments provide evidence that the learned heads capture something different from retrieval-head heuristics.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim that these are genuinely “reasoning heads” is stronger than the evidence supports. The learned gates identify heads important for maintaining benchmark accuracy under a particular streaming-attention compression scheme and reward/training distribution, but this does not establish a general functional role in reasoning.

Efficiency claims are under-measured. The paper reports KV cache sparsity and argues for 20-50% memory reduction, but does not provide direct end-to-end measurements of peak memory, throughput, latency, batching gains, or training overhead versus baselines in realistic serving conditions. This weakens the practical significance of the compression result.

The evaluation is limited to two small distilled reasoning models. It is unclear whether the learned head structure transfers to larger reasoning models, non-distilled models, MoE models, different architectures, longer contexts beyond the tested max lengths, or more diverse reasoning domains.

Some reported improvements over full KV cache, especially on AIME24, are difficult to interpret because AIME has very small sample size and no confidence intervals or multi-seed runs are provided. The paper generally lacks variance estimates, significance testing, or robustness to decoding/prompt choices.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. The paper modifies token-dropping baselines with dynamic allocation and sink/local overhead, uses different attention implementations for different methods, and does not deeply tune all baselines under the same memory or latency objective. Stronger baseline calibration could change the margins.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript provides many hyperparameters, but lacks code release details, exact prompts/templates, answer extraction rules, random seeds, complete threshold-selection procedure, and enough implementation detail for the custom kernels/mixed-attention integration to be straightforwardly reproduced.

The training data construction filters for problems each model already solves correctly, then trains on those; this is sensible for capability preservation but may bias the learned heads toward easier or self-confirming trajectories. The paper does not sufficiently analyze sensitivity to this filtering or possible benchmark/data contamination from DeepScaleR-derived sources.

The presentation is mostly understandable but has recurring terminology/formatting issues and occasional overclaiming, for example treating “near lossless” loosely despite nontrivial drops on some benchmarks and sparsity levels. The limitations section is framed as future work rather than a candid account of current empirical limits.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: KV-cache compression for long chain-of-thought reasoning models, where existing long-context compression methods may fail differently than on instruction models.

The proposed mechanism is conceptually simple and plausible: learn per-head gates between full and local attention under a reward-plus-sparsity objective, then preserve the highest-scoring heads at inference.

The manuscript includes comparisons against token-dropping and head-reallocation baselines across two 7B/8B reasoning models and four benchmarks, plus ablations for adaptive penalty weighting, self-distillation sampling, and L1 strength.
The error-mode analysis and head replacement experiments are useful attempts to go beyond aggregate accuracy and understand why reasoning-model compression fails.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims near-lossless 20-50% cache reduction, but the complete tables show substantial degradation at moderate/high sparsity on several settings, e.g. Llama AIME24 drops from 36.7 to 20.0 at 0.6, Qwen Math500 drops from 87.8 to 71.4 at 0.6, and most 0.8-sparsity results collapse. The strongest claim is only supported at cherry-picked task-specific sparsity thresholds.

The evaluation is narrow: only two small DeepSeek-R1-distilled models are tested, with training on mathematical reasoning data and evaluation mostly on math benchmarks. The only non-math task is MBPP, and there are no larger models, no non-distilled reasoning models, no long-context QA/retrieval tasks, and no realistic serving workloads with batching.

The paper does not convincingly demonstrate actual system benefit. It reports KV-cache sparsity/accuracy but provides no measured wall-clock latency, throughput, batch-size scaling, peak GPU memory, or end-to-end serving results. This is a major gap for an efficiency paper.

Baseline fairness and implementation details are insufficiently convincing. The authors modify H2O/R-KV budgets, use different attention implementations for baselines versus RLKV, and do not compare to all closely related head-selection methods in a fully controlled way. It is unclear whether gains come from the learned head ranking, the budget accounting, local window choices, or implementation differences.

The methodology has several under-specified or questionable choices: training uses 128 sink/256 local tokens but evaluation uses 16/64; inference hard-selects top-k heads after training soft gates; the definition of “KV Cache Budget Sparsity” is not precise enough for GQA architectures; and the adaptive penalty/reward thresholding introduces several tuned heuristics.

The evidence for discovering distinct “reasoning heads” is not strong enough. The replacement experiment shows that heads selected by the method are important under the same compression mechanism, but it does not establish a functional mechanistic distinction from general importance, task-specific math heads, or heads selected by alternative optimization criteria.

Statistical reliability is weak. Results appear to be single-run without confidence intervals or seed variation. Claims of improvements over full KV cache on AIME24 are especially fragile because AIME has very small sample size, so +3.3 or +6.7 percentage points may correspond to one or two examples.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives some hyperparameters and hardware details, but does not clearly commit to releasing code, trained gates, exact prompts, seeds, evaluation scripts, or baseline implementations. RL training with AReaL/SGLang and custom kernels would be hard to reproduce from the manuscript alone.

Presentation is generally readable but sometimes imprecise and promotional. Strong statements such as “lossless reasoning capability,” “systematically identify which heads matter,” and “state-of-the-art compression performance” are not adequately qualified by the limitations visible in the tables.

Limitations and ethics are minimally treated. The paper has a future-work section but lacks a clear limitations section discussing small-model scope, benchmark contamination/overlap risks, evaluation variance, or deployment risks from altered reasoning behavior under compression. Ethical concerns are not major, but the treatment is superficial.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely deployment bottleneck for reasoning LLMs: long chain-of-thought generation makes KV cache memory a major practical constraint. The framing that reasoning models stress existing KV compression methods differently from instruct models is well motivated.

The proposed RLKV method is technically sensible: learn per-head gates between full and streaming/local attention, optimize them with a verifiable RL reward plus sparsity pressure, then preserve the highest-gated heads at inference. This is a clean way to connect head allocation to actual reasoning outcomes rather than proxy retrieval behavior.

The empirical results are promising. Across two 7B/8B reasoning models and GSM8K, Math500, AIME24, and MBPP, RLKV generally outperforms H2O, R-KV, and DuoAttention, especially around 40-60% sparsity where baselines degrade more sharply. The full numerical appendix is useful.

The paper includes meaningful analyses beyond headline accuracy: motivation experiments contrasting instruct vs reasoning models, error mode analyses, head-importance masking experiments comparing reasoning heads to retrieval/random heads, and ablations for adaptive penalty weighting, self-distillation sampling, and L1 strength.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported by implementation details, hyperparameters, training data construction, decoding settings, local attention windows, hardware, and full result tables. The declared LLM use is limited to writing polish and does not raise obvious ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The scope of evidence is still somewhat narrow: only two small distilled reasoning models are evaluated, both in the 7B/8B class and both derived from DeepSeek-R1-style distillation. It is unclear whether the identified reasoning-head phenomenon and learned gates transfer to larger models, different architectures, MoE models, or non-distilled reasoning models.

The central claim of 20-50% near-lossless compression is plausible but not fully nailed down. Several reported improvements over full KV cache occur on small/noisy benchmarks such as AIME24, and there are no confidence intervals or repeated runs, making it hard to distinguish real effects from decoding/evaluation variance.

The paper focuses mostly on accuracy versus nominal KV sparsity, but gives limited direct systems evidence. Actual peak memory, throughput, latency, batching gains, and kernel overheads are not reported in enough detail, even though practical serving efficiency is a major motivation.

The comparison set is reasonable but incomplete. KV quantization, hybrid quantization-plus-head-allocation, and more recent long-context or reasoning-efficiency methods are treated as orthogonal or omitted from direct comparison, leaving some uncertainty about the best practical baseline.

The method requires RL-style training per model and appears to use task-specific mathematical correctness rewards for head discovery. The cost, robustness, and portability of this training step are not fully characterized, especially for domains without verifiable rewards.

The mechanistic interpretation of 'reasoning heads' is interesting but somewhat overstated. Masking/compression sensitivity shows causal importance under this intervention, but does not fully establish a stable functional category distinct from other task-critical heads across prompts, domains, and models.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: KV-cache compression for reasoning LLMs, where long chain-of-thought decoding makes standard compression fragile. The framing around reasoning-specific head importance is useful and clearly motivated by comparisons between instruct and reasoning variants.

The proposed method is technically plausible and reasonably simple: learn per-layer/per-head gates over full versus local attention using GRPO with an L1 sparsity pressure, then deploy by preserving full KV cache only for high-scoring heads. The stabilization techniques are well motivated by the sparse-reward/dense-penalty conflict.

The empirical evaluation is fairly broad for this area, covering three reasoning models, math, code, and MMLU-Pro subsets, multiple sparsity levels, and several relevant baselines including H2O, R-KV, and DuoAttention. The appendix provides extensive numerical tables.

Results show meaningful gains over baselines at moderate compression levels, especially around 0.4-0.6 sparsity on Math500, MBPP, and several MMLU-Pro subsets. The error-mode and head-sensitivity analyses add insight beyond raw accuracy.

Reproducibility is better than average in terms of reported training details: the paper gives model/dataset choices, hardware, batch size, optimizer settings, GRPO sampling settings, sink/local token sizes, prompt template, and training cost.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim that RLKV identifies 'reasoning-critical heads' is only partially supported. The definition is operational, and the evidence is mainly performance under compression plus sensitivity plots. This is useful, but it does not establish that these heads are intrinsically responsible for reasoning rather than being heads that happen to be important under the chosen local-attention compression/training setup.

The evaluation has several ambiguities that affect soundness. The meaning of 'KV cache budget sparsity' is not always intuitive, and the dynamic-budget treatment for H2O/R-KV is nonstandard. Appendix F discusses using full-output lengths for budget estimation in some comparisons, which raises concerns about oracle information or at least about whether all methods are being compared under deployable and identical constraints.

The speedup evidence is weaker than the accuracy evidence. Table 2 compares different batch sizes at similar memory rather than equal-batch single-request latency, and the claimed end-to-end speedups are modest. The paper would benefit from clearer throughput-versus-latency reporting in a real serving engine with continuous batching, since the current implementation details make the practical efficiency claim less decisive.

Several claims of 'near-lossless' or improvement over full KV cache are not statistically supported. AIME24 has only 30 examples, and no confidence intervals, seeds, or variance estimates are reported. Some improvements over the full baseline are likely within noise or decoding variability.

Ablations are limited: most are on Math500 with Qwen-2.5-7B-R1 only. The paper does not fully separate the contributions of RL optimization, self-distillation data filtering, adaptive penalty weighting, and simple supervised/proxy alternatives for head ranking across all models.

Generalization remains somewhat constrained. The method is trained on filtered math problems that the model already solves, then evaluated mostly on math-like reasoning plus selected knowledge subsets. It is unclear how stable the learned heads are across prompts, decoding settings, longer contexts, larger models, multi-turn/chat workloads, or domains with different reasoning styles.

Reproducibility is incomplete without released code, learned head masks/gating scores, seeds, and the exact sampled training/evaluation subsets. The implementation depends on AReaL, SGLang, FlashAttention, block-sparse kernels, and custom attention modifications, so small missing details could materially affect replication.

The paper does not contain a meaningful limitations or ethics discussion. The future-work section mentions extensions, but there is little discussion of failure cases, deployment risks from degraded reasoning under compression, or how incorrect compressed generations should be detected in high-stakes settings.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: KV-cache compression for long chain-of-thought reasoning, where standard token-dropping methods plausibly fail more severely than in short instruct-model decoding.

The proposed head-level RL probing idea is interesting and reasonably original: using reward from actual generations to identify heads whose full-cache access matters is a useful direction beyond retrieval-head heuristics.

The empirical scope is broader than many efficiency papers, covering three reasoning models, several math/code benchmarks, MMLU-Pro subsets, multiple sparsity levels, and comparisons to H2O, R-KV, and DuoAttention.

The appendix provides many implementation details, including training data construction, hyperparameters, hardware, training cost, prompt template, and baseline modifications, which helps reproducibility.
The paper includes useful diagnostic analyses of head sensitivity, response length, and failure modes, which make the contribution more informative than a pure benchmark comparison.
weaknesses: The central interpretability claim that the learned heads are genuinely “reasoning-critical” is overclaimed. The evidence mostly shows that preserving heads selected by the method improves compressed inference; it does not convincingly establish that these heads specifically implement reasoning rather than reflecting task-, model-, reward-, or compression-scheme-specific sensitivity.

The evaluation has several methodological weaknesses. Results are reported without variance, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds, despite small benchmarks such as AIME24 with only 30 examples where changes of a few examples are presented as meaningful gains.

The training data is filtered from DeepScaleR by selecting problems each model already solves, but the manuscript does not provide a contamination or overlap analysis with GSM8K/Math500/AIME-style evaluations. This weakens claims of generalization, especially for math benchmarks.

The “near-lossless” framing is not fully supported. Some table entries labeled under near-lossless thresholds still show nontrivial drops, such as Llama GSM8K at -2.3 and Qwen-3 MBPP at -3.2, while performance collapses at high sparsity such as 0.8 on many tasks.

The comparison protocol for baselines is complicated and may not be fully fair or standard. The dynamic-budget reinterpretation changes H2O/R-KV behavior substantially, and the paper does not clearly separate feasible online budget allocation from use of full-output lengths in analysis.

The speedup evidence is modest relative to the headline memory-compression claims. End-to-end speedups are only 1.09x-1.21x in a vanilla pipeline, and the paper relies on future custom kernels or engine integration for larger practical benefits.

The MBPP evaluation is under-specified and possibly inappropriate: the paper states regex final-answer extraction is used for all datasets, but MBPP normally requires execution-based correctness, so it is unclear whether coding results are reliable.

Ablations are limited: they are performed mainly on one model and one benchmark, and they do not fully isolate whether RL is necessary compared with simpler supervised, gradient-based, perturbation, or validation-set search methods for head ranking.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper names AReaL, SGLang, block-sparse attention, and custom Triton decoding kernels, but does not clearly commit to releasing code, learned head masks, exact seeds, or scripts for reproducing the modified baselines.

Presentation is uneven. Some figures are visually dense, Table 2 is hard to parse, there are cross-reference and grammar issues, and the references/appendix formatting appears rough. These issues do not destroy the paper but reduce confidence in the experimental reporting.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: KV cache compression for long chain-of-thought reasoning, where standard token-dropping and retrieval-head methods can fail badly.

The core idea is original and compelling: use RL with sparse per-head gating as a probe for which KV heads need full-cache access, then turn the learned gates into a head-reallocation compression policy.

The evaluation is broad for a systems/efficiency paper: three reasoning models, math, code, and MMLU-Pro subsets, comparisons to H2O, R-KV, and DuoAttention, plus appendix tables over multiple sparsity levels.

The empirical results are convincing overall. RLKV often preserves near-full accuracy at 20-50% sparsity and substantially outperforms baselines at moderate sparsity, especially on Math500/AIME/MBPP where reasoning degradation is most visible.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond headline accuracy: head sensitivity, error-mode breakdowns, response length, component ablations, and end-to-end memory/latency measurements. These support the claim that the learned heads differ from retrieval heads and matter for reasoning behavior.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: the manuscript reports training data construction, model/dataset choices, hyperparameters, hardware, training cost, decoding settings, prompt template, and baseline implementation adjustments.
weaknesses: The causal interpretation of 'reasoning-critical heads' is somewhat stronger than the evidence fully supports. The method identifies heads useful under this specific local-attention compression and RL objective; it is less clear that these heads are intrinsically responsible for reasoning across compression schemes, prompts, or model families.

The evaluation is limited to relatively small open reasoning models, up to 8B parameters. It is unclear whether the same head sparsity structure, training cost, and accuracy-speed tradeoff hold for larger models or production-scale serving settings.

Some reported gains on small benchmarks, especially AIME24 with only about 30 examples, correspond to one or two examples and are not accompanied by confidence intervals, seeds, or variance estimates. This makes the apparent improvements over full cache or close baselines less reliable.

The speedup evidence is useful but narrow: end-to-end results are reported only for Llama-3.1-8B-R1 on Math500 at sparsity 0.5 in a vanilla PyTorch/Transformers setup. The practical benefit in continuous batching engines, with custom kernels, or under realistic serving loads remains mostly projected.

The training procedure requires per-model RL-style adapter training using filtered problems the model can already solve. The paper does not fully analyze sensitivity to the training corpus, possible benchmark overlap through DeepScaleR-derived data, or transfer when the deployment domain differs substantially from the math-heavy training set.

Although the appendix gives many implementation details, the paper does not appear to provide code or trained head masks. Reproducing the custom mixed-attention/RL pipeline and baseline modifications may still be nontrivial.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck for reasoning LLMs: KV cache growth during long chain-of-thought decoding. The motivation is clear and the distinction between token-dropping failures and head-reallocation failures is compelling.

The core idea is original and technically interesting: using on-policy RL with sparse head gates as a probe for identifying heads whose full KV access matters for generated reasoning outcomes, rather than relying on teacher-forced loss or retrieval-oriented proxy metrics.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this problem setting, covering three reasoning models, math/code/knowledge benchmarks, long-context LongReason evaluation, multiple sparsity levels, and comparisons against H2O, R-KV, DuoAttention, and KVZip.

The method shows meaningful practical gains: near-lossless performance at 20-60% KV cache reduction in many settings and an end-to-end SGLang continuous-batching speedup up to 2.06x at 60% sparsity on Math500.

The paper includes useful ablations for adaptive penalty weighting, self-distillation sampling, beta choice, and sink/local window size, as well as error-mode and head-sensitivity analyses that help explain the observed behavior.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: the manuscript gives training data construction, hardware, optimizer settings, sequence lengths, sink/local sizes, reward setup, baseline modifications, and training cost. The limitations section is honest about static gates, task/model variation, and degradation at very high sparsity.
weaknesses: The mechanistic claim that the selected heads are genuinely 'reasoning-critical' is somewhat overinterpreted. The evidence shows these heads are critical under this specific compression intervention and training objective, but does not fully establish that they are generally responsible for reasoning rather than for robustness to the chosen local-attention approximation, GQA grouping, or decoding setup.

The evaluation is limited to small or mid-sized open reasoning models, mostly 4B-8B distilled/thinking variants. It is unclear whether the same head sparsity patterns and compression frontier transfer to larger frontier-scale reasoning models or substantially different architectures.

Several reported improvements over full KV cache are likely within evaluation noise, especially on AIME24 with very small sample size. The paper does not report confidence intervals, repeated runs, or seed sensitivity for training/evaluation, despite noting nondeterminism in the SGLang engine.

The speedup evidence is promising but narrow: the main end-to-end serving result is for one model/task/hardware setting, and the implementation currently lacks some SGLang production features such as radix-cache reuse or paged attention for the compressed-head buffer.

The method requires per-model RL-based adapter training using filtered problems the model can already solve, which is modest but still a nontrivial setup cost. The paper could better quantify how often gates must be retrained across domains, prompts, decoding policies, or model checkpoints.

Baseline fairness is mostly discussed, but some choices could affect conclusions: token-dropping baselines are modified with dynamic budgets, accuracy results use different engines for different benchmark groups, and not all baselines appear equally optimized for the reasoning-specific long-generation setting.

The ethics/impact discussion is adequate for an efficiency paper but brief; it mainly notes environmental benefits and possible performance degradation, without much discussion of deployment risks from silent reasoning degradation in high-stakes applications.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: KV-cache compression for reasoning models, where long chain-of-thought generation makes naive token dropping brittle.
The core idea of using reward-guided optimization of per-head gates as a probe for compression sensitivity is interesting and potentially useful.

The evaluation covers several models and task families, including math, code, MMLU-Pro subsets, and a long-context LongReason setting, and compares against both token-dropping and head-reallocation baselines.

The paper includes useful ablations for adaptive penalty weighting, self-distillation sampling, regularization strength, and sink/local window size, plus some analysis of error modes and response lengths.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim that the method identifies heads that “matter for reasoning” is not convincingly supported. The learned gates identify heads useful for preserving task accuracy under this specific compression/training setup, but the evidence does not establish that these heads are intrinsically reasoning-critical rather than artifacts of the reward, data, window size, sparsity target, or implementation.

The evaluation protocol raises fairness and realism concerns. The dynamic-budget discussion for H2O/R-KV appears to rely on full-output lengths or oracle-like per-sample information, which is not available before generation in deployment. This makes it hard to interpret comparisons against baselines.

The empirical gains are less decisive than claimed. Some results show substantial degradation at higher sparsity, and KVZip or DuoAttention are competitive or better in multiple cells. The “near-lossless” framing is stretched, especially when deltas of several points and small-sample improvements are treated as meaningful.

Statistical reliability is weak. AIME has only 30 examples, MMLU-Pro uses random subsets of up to 500 examples, and the paper reports no confidence intervals, variance across seeds, or repeated runs despite acknowledging nondeterminism in SGLang.

The speedup evaluation is too narrow. It is reported only for RLKV versus full attention on one model/task/server setting, with changing concurrency levels and no comparable end-to-end measurements for baselines. This does not fully substantiate the deployment-efficiency claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The method depends on custom AReaL/SGLang integration, mixed attention, Triton kernels, and engine-specific behavior, but the manuscript does not provide enough implementation detail or evidence of code release to make the results readily reproducible.

The training/evaluation separation is underspecified. The adapters are trained on filtered DeepScaleR math problems, but the paper does not adequately rule out overlap or contamination with math evaluation benchmarks, nor does it analyze sensitivity to the chosen 3k self-distillation set.

The ablations are limited, mostly centered on one model/dataset, and do not isolate several important design choices such as reward definition, thresholding/top-k discretization, training window versus inference window mismatch, or task-specific versus cross-task head transfer.

Presentation is generally readable, but several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially “first to identify” reasoning-critical heads, “state-of-the-art” compression, and broad generalization from 8K training to 70K inference.

The limitations section is honest about static gates and high-sparsity failures, but it does not address the most serious methodological concerns: oracle-like budgeting, lack of uncertainty estimates, limited reproducibility, and the gap between compression sensitivity and mechanistic reasoning interpretation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely deployment bottleneck for reasoning LLMs: KV-cache growth during long chain-of-thought decoding. The framing that reasoning models are more fragile to token-dropping than instruct models is well motivated and supported by the motivation study and error-mode analysis.

The core idea is technically sensible and fairly original: using on-policy RL signals as a probe to identify heads whose full-cache access matters for reasoning quality, then converting the learned gates into a head-level cache allocation policy. This goes beyond static attention/retrieval-head heuristics and is well aligned with the autoregressive nature of reasoning failures.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this problem setting: three reasoning models, math/code/knowledge benchmarks, LongReason long-context transfer, multiple sparsity levels, and comparisons to H2O, R-KV, DuoAttention, and KVZip. The complete tables show consistent gains at moderate sparsity, often preserving near-full accuracy with 20-60% cache reduction.

The paper includes useful ablations of adaptive penalty weighting, self-distillation sampling, beta, and sink/local window size, plus qualitative analyses of head sensitivity, error modes, and response length. These analyses make the mechanism more convincing than a raw benchmark-only paper.

The systems evaluation is a meaningful addition: integrating into SGLang and reporting up to 2.06x end-to-end speedup under continuous batching makes the contribution more practically relevant than a purely theoretical memory reduction.

Presentation is generally clear. The method, experimental settings, training cost, hyperparameters, baseline adaptations, and limitations are described in enough detail to make the main claims understandable and likely reproducible with moderate effort.
weaknesses: Some central mechanistic language is stronger than the evidence warrants. The learned heads are shown to be causally important under this compression intervention, but calling them the primary carriers of CoT consistency or reasoning mechanisms may overinterpret a task/model-specific gating artifact.

The evidence for improvements over full KV cache is not statistically grounded. Several reported positive deltas are small and may reflect decoding/evaluation variance, especially on AIME24 with only 30 examples where 3.3 percentage points is one sample. Confidence intervals or repeated runs would make the claims more reliable.

The speedup evaluation is relatively narrow: it is reported mainly for Math500 on Llama-3.1-8B-R1 on one A100 setting. The paper would be stronger with speed/memory results across more models, sequence lengths, batch regimes, and comparisons to optimized baseline implementations, not just accuracy baselines.

Baseline fairness is mostly discussed, but still somewhat delicate. H2O/R-KV are modified to use dynamic budgets and run with eager attention because they require attention scores, while DuoAttention/RLKV use flash attention; this is reasonable for accuracy but complicates direct practical efficiency comparisons.

The method requires per-model RL adapter training, with tens of GPU-hours per model. This is modest compared with LLM training, but it is still a nontrivial deployment cost, and the paper does not deeply analyze how reusable the learned gates are across tasks, prompts, decoding settings, or model variants.

The training data construction filters for problems already solved correctly by the model, which stabilizes reward signals but may bias the identified heads toward preserving existing successful behavior rather than robustly handling hard or unfamiliar reasoning trajectories.

Reproducibility is adequate but not complete: implementation details and hyperparameters are provided, but the manuscript does not clearly commit to releasing code, trained gates, exact sampled subsets, or SGLang integration patches. Reproducing the systems results may require substantial engineering.

The limitations section is honest about static gates, task/model variation, and high-sparsity degradation, but the ethics/impact discussion is thin. Efficiency work can broaden access to powerful reasoning models, which is positive, but the paper could more explicitly address dual-use acceleration and evaluation reliability when compressed reasoning silently changes outputs.
